strengths: High relevance and timeliness: LLM leaderboards such as Chatbot Arena have become standard benchmarks for evaluating state-of-the-art models, making an audit of their statistical stability of great interest to the AI community.

Methodological soundness: Adapting Approximate Maximum Influence Perturbation (AMIP) to the Bradley–Terry setting and combining it with an exact refit verification step ensures that all reported ranking flips are true positives (exact witnesses of non-robustness).

Comprehensive empirical scope: The paper evaluates multiple evaluation platforms (Chatbot Arena, Vision, Search, WebDev, MT-Bench), compares human vs. LLM judges, includes bootstrap confidence intervals and uniform subsampling controls, and provides non-LLM reference points (NBA and ATP tennis).

Qualitative inspection: Analyzing the specific dropped pairs provides valuable diagnostic insights, showing that ranking flips are frequently driven by rare, anomalous upset losses to significantly lower-ranked models.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The technical approach is largely a straightforward application of existing statistical influence techniques (AMIP from Broderick et al., 2020 and logistic regression influence functions from Pregibon, 1981) to the Bradley–Terry model.

Expected statistical phenomena: When two models have overlapping confidence intervals and marginal score gaps (e.g., GPT-4-0125-preview vs. GPT-4-1106-preview), it is statistically expected that removing a couple of high-leverage upset outcomes will flip their point estimates. While the exact percentage (0.003%) is striking, the underlying cause is simply narrow score separation and high leverage.

Actionable solutions are high-level: The proposed remedies in the discussion (e.g., prompt filtering, expert annotations, eliciting confidence) are intuitive best practices rather than tested algorithmic solutions integrated into the ranking pipeline.

strengths: Highly timely and significant topic: As the AI community heavily relies on crowdsourced leaderboards (e.g., Chatbot Arena) to benchmark frontier LLMs, rigorously evaluating the statistical robustness and fragility of these rankings is of paramount importance.

Principled and efficient methodology: Adapting the Approximate Maximum Influence Perturbation (AMIP) framework to both weighted and unweighted Bradley–Terry (logistic regression) formulations provides a computationally fast method to discover worst-case drop subsets without combinatorial search.
Definitive verification: The method avoids false positives by explicitly refitting the Bradley–Terry model on the pruned data to confirm that the ranking flip genuinely occurs.

Extensive and compelling empirical evaluation: The study evaluates multiple LLM arenas across modalities and domains (Chatbot Arena, Vision Arena, Webdev, Search Arena, MT-Bench), contrasts human vs. LLM-as-a-judge annotators, compares against sports baselines (NBA, ATP tennis), and evaluates bootstrap confidence intervals.

Insightful analysis of sensitivity: The finding that dropping just 2 out of ~57,000 matches (0.003%) alters the #1 rank in Chatbot Arena—and that the dropped pairs correspond to anomalous/outlier human judgments—provides clear, actionable takeaways for leaderboard design.
weaknesses: Moderate algorithmic novelty: The algorithmic framework is essentially a direct application of existing influence function techniques (AMIP and additive one-step Newton) to the standard logistic regression formulation of Bradley–Terry models.

Statistical intuition vs. surprisingness: It is well known in paired comparison modeling that when two items have very close estimated scores, their relative ordering has high variance. While the authors demonstrate this convincingly via Figure 18 and bootstrap analysis, the paper could better contextualize how much of this sensitivity is simply an artifact of reporting discrete ranks on top of statistically indistinguishable point estimates.

Curious model attribution in qualitative inspection: In Section F and footnote 8, the authors refer to evaluating prompt pairs using 'GPT-5.1' accessed via ChatGPT incognito mode. Clarification is needed regarding the exact model version used, as 'GPT-5.1' is not a standard publicly documented release.

strengths: High relevance and timeliness: LLM evaluation leaderboards (notably Chatbot Arena) serve as primary benchmarks for industry and academic model development. Demonstrating their statistical fragility under worst-case perturbations is an important contribution to the community.

Sound and efficient methodology: Adapting the Approximate Maximum Influence Perturbation (AMIP) framework to the Bradley–Terry logistic regression formulation provides a computationally tractable way (O(N log(αN) + NP^2 + P^3)) to identify influential subsets without intractable combinatorial search.

Rigorous verification: The proposed pipeline does not rely solely on the first-order Taylor approximation; it explicitly refits the Bradley–Terry model on the pruned data to guarantee zero false positives for any reported ranking change.

Comprehensive empirical analysis: The authors evaluate multiple benchmark arenas (Chatbot Arena, Vision Arena, Search Arena, WebDev Arena, MT-Bench) alongside sports baselines (NBA, ATP), systematically analyzing the effects of sample sizes, human vs. LLM judges, uniform vs. worst-case deletion, and bootstrap confidence intervals.

Insightful qualitative analysis: The paper inspects the specific dropped preferences responsible for the top flips (e.g., in Chatbot Arena), demonstrating that anomalous/outlier judgments where vastly inferior models defeated top models are the primary culprits.
weaknesses: Predictable sensitivity for tightly clustered scores: From a classical statistics perspective, it is expected that point-estimate rankings are fragile when score differences between top competitors are minuscule (e.g., GPT-4-0125-preview vs. GPT-4-1106-preview). While the authors test bootstrap intervals, standard practice in statistics already treats overlapping intervals as tied.

Susceptibility to masking and false negatives: Because AMIP relies on additive first-order approximations, it can suffer from masking effects where groups of points are influential only in combination (as acknowledged in Appendix H). While this does not undermine the reported positive flips, it means failure to find an adversarial subset does not guarantee robustness.

Lack of empirical evaluation of proposed defenses: While Section 6 offers sensible design recommendations (e.g., eliciting confidence ratings, prompt filtering, outlier removal), the paper does not empirically evaluate whether applying these filters restores robustness on the studied arenas.

strengths: Highly relevant and timely topic: As LLM leaderboards (such as LMSYS Chatbot Arena) heavily influence community perception and development priorities, auditing the stability and robustness of Bradley–Terry (BT) leaderboards is an important research problem.

Methodologically sound and computationally efficient: Adapting Approximate Maximum Influence Perturbation (AMIP) via first-order influence functions avoids combinatorial search, and the inclusion of an exact refitting verification step ensures no false positives are reported.
Clear writing and presentation: The mathematical setup connecting Bradley–Terry modeling to standard logistic regression diagnostics is clean, straightforward, and easy to follow.
Diagnostic utility: The qualitative inspection of dropped matchups and prompt types illustrates how influence scores can serve as a concrete auditing tool to inspect high-leverage evaluation items.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The core technique directly applies existing first-order influence function formulas for logistic regression (Pregibon, 1981; Broderick et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2024) to the standard logistic formulation of the Bradley–Terry model. The algorithmic contribution beyond established AMIP workflows is minimal.

Lack of contextualization with statistical uncertainty / confidence intervals: The fact that dropping a tiny number of matchups can flip the top-1 ranking is largely a consequence of the top two models having overlapping confidence intervals and nearly identical point estimates (a difference of only 0.034 in BT score). Platforms like Chatbot Arena report bootstrap confidence intervals precisely because rank orderings among closely clustered models are not statistically distinguishable. The paper treats point estimate flips as unexpected sensitivity without sufficiently analyzing whether these flips occur within standard confidence intervals.

Confounded comparison between Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench: The manuscript claims MT-Bench is substantially more robust than Chatbot Arena (3.22% vs. 0.02% of data dropped to flip top-1). However, MT-Bench evaluates only a handful of models (6 models shown in Fig. 5) with an enormous score gap between rank 1 and rank 2 (~0.53), whereas Chatbot Arena contains dozens of top-tier models with tiny gaps (~0.03). As the authors note in Figure 6, sensitivity is directly driven by score proximity; attributing MT-Bench's higher robustness to 'expert annotators' and 'higher quality prompts' is an uncontrolled comparison.

Divergence from leaderboard implementations in practice: Real-world Chatbot Arena leaderboards explicitly handle ties via paired/weighted entries, whereas this analysis discards ties entirely. While the authors acknowledge this difference in Section 3.1, ties constitute a substantial fraction of human evaluation battles, and discarding them may artificially increase sensitivity.

strengths: Highly relevant and timely problem: LLM preference leaderboards (such as Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench) heavily influence the AI community, making rigorous auditing of their statistical robustness and stability of paramount importance.

Methodologically sound and computationally efficient: Applying influence-function-based Approximate Maximum Influence Perturbation (AMIP) to the Bradley–Terry logistic regression framework avoids intractable combinatorial search, allowing fast identification and exact verification (via refitting) of worst-case subsets.

Actionable and concrete empirical findings: Demonstrates that dropping as few as 9 comparisons (0.02% of data) can alter the #1 model in Chatbot Arena, highlights that MT-Bench is substantially more robust to worst-case dropping, and reveals that dropped matchups predominantly involve the contested models directly.
Clear, structured writing with thorough appendix detailing the influence calculations and individual game inspection.
weaknesses: Limited contextualization with statistical uncertainty (confidence intervals): The paper frames the flipping of top-ranked models as severe fragility, but for models with virtually identical point estimates (e.g., GPT-4-0125 vs GPT-4-1106, separated by only ~0.034 in BT score and a 55% win rate), point estimates are known to fall within bootstrap confidence intervals. It is not clear whether dropping a small fraction of data flips models that are genuinely statistically distinguishable at standard confidence levels (e.g., 95% CI), or whether this sensitivity merely reflects expected sampling noise between near-identical models.

Modest technical novelty: The paper is primarily an application of established tools (AMIP from Broderick et al., 2020 and classical logistic regression influence functions from Pregibon, 1981) to Bradley–Terry models. Proposition 3.1 is an elementary property of top-k sets rather than a substantial theoretical contribution.

Discrepancies from real-world platform pipelines: As acknowledged in Section 3.1, the analysis discards ties, whereas platforms like Chatbot Arena incorporate ties via weighted symmetric entries. Modern leaderboard practices also increasingly employ style-control covariates and bootstrap ranking distributions, which are not evaluated under this auditing framework.

Dataset scale and temporal scope: The experiments are performed on historical snapshots (~55k votes for Chatbot Arena, ~3.3k for MT-Bench). Chatbot Arena currently operates at millions of votes. The manuscript would be strengthened by analyzing how the critical drop fraction $\alpha$ scales asymptotically with dataset size $N$ for a fixed BT difference.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant topic: Evaluating the stability and robustness of Bradley–Terry (BT) leaderboards (such as Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench) is of high importance to the AI community given their central role in model evaluation.

Sound methodological adaptation: Framing the BT model as logistic regression and applying Approximate Maximum Influence Perturbation (AMIP) offers a computationally efficient way to audit ranking stability without combinatorial search.
Empirical verification: The framework avoids false positives by refitting the BT model after identifying candidate influential matchups to confirm actual rank reversals.
Clear writing and presentation: The paper is well-structured, easy to follow, and provides transparent explanations of the mathematical formulation and runtime characteristics.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The technique is a direct application of the AMIP framework (Broderick et al., 2020) and standard logistic regression influence functions (Pregibon, 1981). Proposition 3.1 is an elementary mathematical fact about finite sorted sets rather than a substantial theoretical contribution.

Confounding ranking flips with statistical insignificance: The finding that dropping ~9 matchups can flip the top-1 and top-2 models is largely an artifact of the two models having virtually identical estimated BT scores (a difference of 0.034, as shown in Figure 1). Chatbot Arena and similar platforms routinely compute bootstrap confidence intervals showing that adjacent models frequently overlap within error margins. The paper does not adequately benchmark against or discuss existing bootstrap uncertainty quantification.

Discrepancies with real-world leaderboard implementations: Real-world Chatbot Arena leaderboards incorporate ties (which make up a substantial proportion of user votes) and often adjust for style/length biases. Discarding ties in the analysis weakens the direct applicability of the conclusions to the actual live platform.

Evaluation on relatively small historical snapshots: The experiments rely on an older snapshot of ~57k evaluations (and MT-Bench with ~3.3k), whereas current leaderboards operate on millions of votes. It remains unclear how data-dropping sensitivity scales as total comparisons and model connectivity grow substantially larger.

Limited actionable remedies: While Section 5 discusses potential directions (e.g., confidence elicitation, routing), the paper does not empirically evaluate any proposed robust ranking estimator or aggregation mechanism to mitigate the observed sensitivity.
